/society/2026/nov/17/alan-milburn-tax-cu.headline: Ministers vow to create new welfare system for young people as they back Milburn report
/society/2026/nov/17/alan-milburn-tax-cu.excerpt: Ministers have promised to create an entirely new welfare system for young people as they gave their backing to Alan Milburn’s 278-page report, promising spending cuts next year to help pay for his proposals and giving him a government role to push them through. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, told his cabinet colleagues on Tuesday morning the report was a “watershed moment” and offered a “comprehensive vision” as he invited its author to address the meeting. He then sat in the Commons in a public display of support as his work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, backed Milburn’s vision of a youth employment system with much more employment support but significantly lower benefit payments. “We need a new settlement for young people,” McFadden said. “This new settlement must give people the best chance of higher living standards for the whole of their lives. It must change the equation that sees us spend £25 on the consequences of inactivity for every pound to be spent on opportunity.” He added that the search for departmental cuts to help pay for the proposals would begin almost immediately. “I have no doubt it will also be an issue in the spending review, but the first thing we should do is reprioritise spending to get more support to young people,” he told MPs.
/society/2026/nov/17/alan-milburn-tax-cu.trail: Government promises spending cuts to pay for the proposals, described by prime minister as ‘watershed moment’

/society/2026/nov/17/alan-milburn-tax-cu.headline: UK unemployment unexpectedly eases to 4.6% as government releases Milburn report
/society/2026/nov/17/alan-milburn-tax-cu.excerpt: The UK unemployment rate has unexpectedly fallen as the government released an important report on the youth jobs crisis. The unemployment rate was 4.6% in September, dipping from 4.7% in August and down from 5% earlier in the year, according to the Office for National Statistics. However, the number of vacancies fell as employers delayed hiring in response to global economic uncertainty and the use of artificial intelligence, which many analysts expect will lead to widespread job losses. Business groups said the slump in vacancies posed a problem for the government as responded to Alan Milburn’s report on young people not in employment, education or training (Neets). Milburn, a former health secretary, unveiled his long-awaited report into youth unemployment on Tuesday morning in London, urging ministers to cut disability and sickness payments for under-25s and invest the money in back-to-work schemes. The British Chambers of Commerce said it was “alarming” that the number of vacancies had tumbled to its lowest level since 2014 and unemployment for 18- to 24-year-olds was nearly triple the average for UK adults, at 13%. “This will put further pressure on today’s Milburn review to deliver a sea change in the government’s approach to tackling youth joblessness,” it said. The number of vacancies dropped to 690,000 in October after soaring to more than 1.3m after the pandemic.
/society/2026/nov/17/alan-milburn-tax-cu.trail: Wage growth falls to 3.5% in September, as ministers examine how best to get young people into work

/society/2026/nov/17/alan-milburn-tax-cu.headline: Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts
/society/2026/nov/17/alan-milburn-tax-cu.excerpt: Almost a million young people – one in eight – in the UK are not in education, employment or training (Neet). Having reached the highest level in a decade, the government is seeking to bring that number down after the recommendations made in Alan Milburn’s landmark report. However, the Neet population is not uniform – making Britain’s youth jobs crisis tougher to respond to. Here we outline the diverse backgrounds of the group struggling to make the transition from school to the world of work on a sustainable basis. The highest level in a decade An estimated 981,000 of 16- to 24-year-olds in the UK are Neet, accounting for 13% of that age group, according to official figures – close to the highest level since 2014. Experts say there are myriad reasons for the high numbers, including the legacies of austerity and the Covid pandemic, rising mental ill health, fewer entry-level jobs, rising costs and taxes for businesses, AI disrupting the jobs market, and employers cutting recruitment as the Middle East war damages Britain’s economy. Unemployment among the under-25s has risen at the fastest rate since the 2008 financial crisis. Young people now make up about 40% of all unemployment. This has compounded by a drop in entry-level jobs: over the last 20 years the number of mid- and lower-skilled positions has fallen by about 1.6m. Higher-skilled jobs have risen by about 6.3m. The Saturday job has declined, and automation and AI are replacing entry-level roles.
/society/2026/nov/17/alan-milburn-tax-cu.trail: Bringing the number not in education, employment or training down from a decade high will be tough. Here’s why

/us-news/2026/nov/17/mary-peltola-alaska.headline: Democrat wins Alaska governor’s seat for first time in nearly 30 years
/us-news/2026/nov/17/mary-peltola-alaska.excerpt: Democrats have captured Alaska’s governor’s seat for the first time in nearly three decades, marking another major victory for their party in a midterm election period that has dramatically shifted political power across the US. Former Alaska state legislator Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republican opponents, including a candidate backed by Donald Trump, becoming the first Democrat elected governor of Alaska since 1998. His victory – called by the Associated Press on Friday, 10 days after the polls closed – adds to a growing list of Democratic gains nationwide, bringing the party’s total to 30 US governorships. Democrats have also taken control of governor’s offices in several other longtime Republican strongholds, including Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas. Kreiss-Tomkins, widely known as JKT, secured the win having mounted a political comeback three years after departing the Alaska house of representatives. The 37-year-old traveled extensively throughout the state during his campaign, building support around economic concerns and a promise to change the direction of Alaska’s government. His platform centered on tackling affordability, ensuring full funding for public education, and requiring all oil and gas producers to pay corporate income taxes. He also pushed for a temporary halt to new datacenter developments until state lawmakers establish regulations governing their construction.
/us-news/2026/nov/17/mary-peltola-alaska.trail: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins’ victory means Democrats will now hold 30 US governorships after midterm blowout

/us-news/2026/nov/17/mary-peltola-alaska.headline: US voters share why they cast their ballots – from frustration with Trump to affordability concerns
/us-news/2026/nov/17/mary-peltola-alaska.excerpt: In the battleground state of Maine, Todd Cox, 63, has supported the state’s incumbent Republican senator Susan Collins not once, but twice, in previous elections. Not this time. On Tuesday, Cox, a technology professional, cast his vote for Collins’s Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson – driven not by pressing local issues, but broader concern “for the direction the country is going in”, he said. “We definitely haven’t become kinder and gentler under this administration,” Cox said. “There’s a lot of bullying that goes on. It goes back to affordability. It’s the war in Iran – that shouldn’t be happening. It’s the disregard for the rule of law. It just seems like they’re thumbing their nose at it.” As millions of people lined up to cast their ballots nationwide, the question looming over Tuesday’s US midterm elections – with control of the US Congress and key checks and balances on Donald Trump at stake – was just how many Americans felt the same way. There were signs of high turnout in this election, with 435 seats in the House of Representatives, 35 of 100 seats in the Senate, 39 governorships and thousands of state legislative seats up for grabs, as well as many local contests and ballot measures on issues including taxes, abortion rights and voting rules. To win control of the US Senate in Washington, Democrats must flip four Republican-held seats and retain all of those currently held by the party.
/us-news/2026/nov/17/mary-peltola-alaska.trail: ‘It’s the disregard for the rule of law. It just seems like they’re thumbing their nose at it’

/us-news/2026/nov/17/mary-peltola-alaska.headline: DoJ tells Democrats in letters they could be targets of Alaska ballot investigation
/us-news/2026/nov/17/mary-peltola-alaska.excerpt: The justice department has sent letters to a top Democratic election lawyer and other Democrats informing them they could be targets in a federal investigation into efforts to get an Alaska man with the same name as Republican senator Daniel Sullivan on to the ballot. The decision to send the letters is very unusual. The justice department has long avoided taking actions that could affect an election close to election day. It is also not common to send out target letters so early in an investigation; receiving a target letter does not mean that a person will be charged with a crime. One letter’s existence was confirmed by a person familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation. A federal grand jury in Alaska is investigating potential conspiracy and donor fraud, according to the New York Times and ABC News. It is not clear how many people received the target letters. The justice department’s Alaska investigation accelerated after a bombshell story in the New York Times revealing that allies of Mary Peltola were behind an effort to get someone with the same name as the incumbent senator from Alaska on the ballot to confuse voters. Eventually they found Daniel J Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher. Peltola and her campaign denied any involvement in the matter, but the Times reported that lawyers for the campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) were involved in the effort.
/us-news/2026/nov/17/mary-peltola-alaska.trail: Top election lawyer and lawmakers received notes over alleged scheme to confuse voters with two Dan Sullivans

/us-news/2026/nov/17/mary-peltola-alaska.headline: Alaska prosecutor investigates alleged Democratic plot to confuse voters with second Dan Sullivan
/us-news/2026/nov/17/mary-peltola-alaska.excerpt: The top federal prosecutor in Alaska confirmed on Friday the existence of a criminal and a civil investigation into an alleged scheme by Democrats to confuse voters by recruiting a spoiler candidate on the ballot for US Senate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent, senator Dan Sullivan. Speaking at a news conference in Anchorage on Friday, US attorney Michael Heyman cited reporting by the New York Times which suggested that the Senate campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola and national Democrats had, in his words, “orchestrated a sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up Daniel J Sullivan as a sham candidate”. Both Dan Sullivans – one a Republican senator and the other a retired schoolteacher with no prior political experience – qualified for the ballot. “We are taking that extremely seriously,” Heyman said. “This new information has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska,” he added. “As we speak, law enforcement around the country are taking investigative steps with respect to a criminal investigation on these matters.” In a separate filing, the Department of Justice asked a federal judge to order state elections officials to isolate ballots ranking Dan J Sullivan to investigate potential voter “confusion” with the incumbent Dan Sullivan. /us-news/2026/nov/17/mary-peltola-alaska.headline: A working-class Alaskan Native takes on a ‘multimillionaire’ Republican for seat in Congress
/us-news/2026/nov/17/mary-peltola-alaska.excerpt: As Republicans fight to maintain their narrow majority in Congress, they face a unique challenge in Alaska – not from a Democrat, but from an independent commercial fisher and first-time candidate running to flip the state’s lone House seat. Bill Hill, who is an Alaska Native and has worked in education and construction, has positioned himself as a working-class candidate who will fight to make life more affordable for people like himself and his family. Like voters across the country, Alaskans are deeply worried about affordability and the rising cost of basic necessities. Hill counts himself among the voters who have felt squeezed by high fuel prices driven up by Donald Trump’s war on Iran. “When the spring fuel barge showed up in my home town of Naknek this spring, I went from paying $118 to fill my truck up to over $200,” Hill said. “Our gas went from $6.70 a gallon to almost $9 a gallon.” Hill’s campaign to unseat the Republican congressman Nick Begich has gained momentum in the final weeks before the 3 November election, as national Democrats line up behind him and ad spending ramps up. The non-partisan Cook Political Report recently shifted the race from “likely Republican” to “leans Republican”, with the district favoring Republicans by six percentage points. Recent polls showed Hill trailing Begich by single digits, but Hill’s support grows when voters learn more about his background, as he works to boost his name recognition.
/us-news/2026/nov/17/mary-peltola-alaska.trail: Independent candidate Bill Hill is threatening to unseat Trump ally Nick Begich with a message of affordability

/uk-news/2026/nov/18/shabana-mahmood-fas.headline: Shabana Mahmood launches review into murder of student Henry Nowak
/uk-news/2026/nov/18/shabana-mahmood-fas.excerpt: Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has launched a review to examine whether opportunities were missed to prevent the murder of the student Henry Nowak. It follows claims that there were several warning signs that the perpetrator, Vickrum Digwa, had a history of threatening behaviour and an obsession with weapons. Nowak, 18, died in December after being fatally stabbed as he walked home from a night out in Southampton. He was handcuffed by police officers while bleeding to death after Digwa falsely accused Nowak of racial abuse. In police body-worn camera footage which prompted a public outcry, Nowak was heard repeatedly saying: “I’ve been stabbed,” to which an officer replied: “Don’t think you have, mate.” Nowak’s death sparked widespread protests, allegations of “two-tier policing” and a spike in racist attacks against the UK’s Sikh community. Digwa, a Sikh, was carrying two knives, including a kirpan, on the night of the killing. Carrying the blade is permitted in the UK for religious purposes. Digwa, 23, has subsequently been accused by young local Sikhs of using threatening behaviour in a Southampton gurdwara, or temple, in the months leading up to the fatal attack on Nowak. The Sun reported that Digwa was seen brandishing an airgun in his back garden in October 2022. A neighbour who recorded him firing shots said she reported this to the police, but Hampshire constabulary was unable to find a record of the incident.
/uk-news/2026/nov/18/shabana-mahmood-fas.trail: Move comes after claims that killer had history of using threatening behaviour and an obsession with weapons

/uk-news/2026/nov/18/shabana-mahmood-fas.headline: Mahmood orders urgent security review after killing of Ann Widdecombe
/uk-news/2026/nov/18/shabana-mahmood-fas.excerpt: Security arrangements for high-profile public figures including politicians and members of the royal family are to be urgently reviewed after the killing of Ann Widdecombe, the home secretary has said. Shabana Mahmood said former MPs, party leaders who are not MPs, peers, former members of devolved parliaments and party spokespeople will also be offered police support. The UK’s protective security system will be re-examined to combat the growing risks of terrorism, extremism and state threats, as well as harassment and intimidation, Mahmood said. The review will be carried out by Sir Stephen Lovegrove, a former UK national security adviser, who will look at whether current security arrangements ensure there is adequate protection for those most at risk. This includes high-profile individuals such as members of the royal family, government ministers, MPs, locally elected representatives and other prominent individuals in British politics. His review will not include an assessment of individual cases. Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokesperson, was found dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries. Joshua Kerry, 28, has been charged with Widdecombe’s murder. He is also accused of “online reconnaissance” of prominent people and institutions, travelling to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage’s home in south London on 19 April 2025 and trying to break into it 15 months before Widdecombe was killed.
/uk-news/2026/nov/18/shabana-mahmood-fas.trail: Home secretary also expands police support ‘with immediate effect’ for high-profile public figures not currently MPs

/uk-news/2026/nov/18/shabana-mahmood-fas.headline: Victims say Home Office attempt to curtail spycops inquiry will result in a ‘cover-up’
/uk-news/2026/nov/18/shabana-mahmood-fas.excerpt: Victims of intrusive police surveillance have accused the government of seeking to cut short the spycops public inquiry that has been examining widespread misconduct committed by undercover officers. The independent judge-led inquiry is scrutinising how officers, who spied on tens of thousands of political activists over more than four decades, carried out abuses such as deceiving women into sexual relationships and fathering children. The inquiry has been running for more than a decade, and is expected to last another two years. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has said she is concerned about the length and cost of the process. It was set up in 2015 and was supposed to have been completed within three years. Latest figures show the inquiry, which has been led by retired judge Sir John Mitting, has so far cost £144m. Mahmood initiated a public consultation, which closes on Sunday, that she said would help determine whether the inquiry should continue in a different format. However, those who were spied on say that the Home Office is looking to severely limit or scrap the later stages, leaving the full extent of wrongdoing by the police hidden. They say more than 2,000 people have objected to what they believe would be a cover-up. The spycops inquiry is one of the longest-running public inquiries.
/uk-news/2026/nov/18/shabana-mahmood-fas.trail: Shabana Mahmood is concerned about length and £144m cost of inquiry into intrusive police surveillance
